oe.title: Ways of representing electrons to explain concepts and reactions
points: Orbital box notation shows spin and Hund's rule/Pauli principle (half-filled stability in Cr/Cu, unpaired electrons → paramagnetism, d-electron counts in complexes).
Spectroscopic notation (1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 …) is compact for writing configurations and predicting blocks/ions (e.g. 4s lost before 3d).
Four quantum numbers (n, l, m_l, m_s) uniquely describe each electron (Pauli exclusion).
Dot-and-cross and Lewis structures count bonding and lone pairs, which feed into VSEPR shapes and dative bonds (ligands).
Curly arrows show movement of electron pairs in mechanisms (nucleophilic substitution, electrophilic addition); fish-hook (half) arrows show homolytic fission and free radicals.

Energy level diagrams explain emission/absorption spectra (E = hf); d-orbital splitting diagrams explain colour of complexes; MO/HOMO–LUMO diagrams explain bonding/antibonding orbitals, bond order and colour of conjugated molecules.
Each representation has limits: no single one is 'most useful'. The best choice depends on the concept being explained.
equations: Bond order = ½(bonding e^− − antibonding e^−)
diagrams: Curly-arrow SN2 mechanism and fish-hook homolytic fission.
Octahedral d-orbital splitting diagram; HOMO–LUMO diagram.

oe.title: Confirming that blue crystals are CuSO_4.5H_2O
points: Water of crystallisation: heat a weighed sample to constant mass (cool in a desiccator). Blue → white anhydrous CuSO_4; the mass loss should match 5H_2O (36.0% water). Adding water back turns it blue again.
Copper: AAS, or colorimetry. Add excess NH_3 to give deep blue [Cu(NH_3)_4(H_2O)_2]^2+ and read from a calibration graph. A flame test gives blue-green.
Sulfate: add BaCl_2(aq) to get a white BaSO_4 precipitate; weigh it (gravimetric) to find % sulfate.
Copper by redox titration: Cu^2+ + excess KI → I_2, titrate with standard thiosulfate (starch indicator). Or complexometric EDTA titration.
Compare % composition with theoretical values (GFM 249.7 g: Cu 25.4%, SO_4 38.5%, H_2O 36.0%).
The colour comes from d–d transitions of Cu^2+ (d^9) in [Cu(H_2O)_6]^2+: it absorbs orange/red light, so it looks blue.
equations: Example: 2.50 g → 1.60 g after heating: water = 0.90 g (0.050 mol), CuSO_4 = 0.0100 mol → ratio 1:5
diagrams: Heating to constant mass with a crucible and desiccator.
d-orbital splitting diagram for octahedral Cu^2+.

3 marks: The maximum available mark would be awarded to a candidate who has demonstrated, at an appropriate level, a good understanding of the chemistry involved. This type of response might include a statement of the principles involved, a relationship or an equation, and the application of these to respond to the context. The answer does not need to be ‘excellent’ or ‘complete’ for the candidate to gain full marks.
